conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks and months after having a baby, because the transition can be a lot harder than most people expect.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and how things have felt for you over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety—in which case we’ll talk through the next steps together.

I’ll ask each question conversationally. If anything feels confusing, just let me know and we’ll pause. When you’re ready, we can start.

Thinking about the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time, but lately it feels like I have to force it. Even when my partner tries to be funny, I just smile to be polite.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can’t really laugh at all. I might give a little smile if someone else is joking, but it doesn’t feel natural—more like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little outings or even just a quiet cup of coffee, but now it all feels kind of… flat. I’ll plan something, thinking it might help, but when the time comes I’m too tired or I just don’t care anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I’m missing some cue. Even when my partner says the baby’s just being a baby, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the baby’s too quiet or the blanket’s too close to his face. I check the monitor again and again, even when I know he’s fine. It’s like my mind keeps jumping to the worst thing that could happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. There’s no real danger—I’m just holding the baby or folding laundry—but it feels like something awful is about to happen. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to get him to nap—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes waiting. I’ll look around the house and just want to cry because it never feels done, and I can’t ever catch my breath.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head starts spinning with everything I didn’t do right or might forget to do tomorrow, and I can’t fall asleep. Even when the baby finally sleeps a longer stretch, I’m still awake, staring at the ceiling or checking the monitor every few minutes.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I tear up at least once a day—sometimes when I’m nursing, sometimes when I’m just looking at him and feel like I’m failing him. It’s this heavy sadness I can’t shake, even when I tell myself I should be happy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried probably three or four times this week. Once was after a phone call with my mom—she asked how I was doing and I just lost it. Other times it’s when the baby won’t settle and I feel useless. The tears come fast and I can’t always explain why.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just feel overwhelmed and sad, not like I want to be gone. I want to be here for my baby—I just wish I could feel better while doing it.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery (per chart)

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked anhedonia, inability to anticipate or experience pleasure (Q2)  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt, self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Psychomotor anxiety: near-daily intrusive worry, catastrophic thoughts, physical panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination, not infant demands (Q7)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Subjective sense of “failing” infant (Q8)  
- Denies self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms, functional impairment evident.  
No suicidal ideation reported → current safety risk low (continue monitoring).

Screening significance: High index of concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; scores would likely exceed clinical cut-offs (EPDS >12).  
Recommend formal diagnostic interview, psychoeducation, support resources, and consideration of expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty.
